items.originalTitle: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
items.summary:
A developer conducted a benchmark to assess the impact of different JavaScript frameworks on AI-assisted development by instructing agents to build a Pokémon app using various frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and SvelteKit. The study measured factors such as development time, token usage, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores using Lighthouse, aiming to provide evidence beyond subjective claims about framework efficiency.

The experiment involved running multiple iterations per framework to account for variability in AI output and performance metrics, using a conformance suite to ensure specification adherence. While the app was relatively simple and content-focused, the study highlights the stochastic nature of AI-generated code and the challenges in fairly comparing frameworks. The results offer insights into the cost, quality, and maintainability of AI-generated frontend code across popular JavaScript frameworks.

A team of five Qwen3.8-27B models running a Memdoor workflow achieved a mean score of 9.8 out of 10 on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, surpassing the 9.6 score of the authors' own harness and 8.0 of Fable 5. The multi-agent system uses distinct roles communicating through files on disk and was tested over five passes with nearly all runs successful.

The workflow replicated the authors' exact prompts and method, running on OpenRouter hosts with a 128K token limit and costing about $0.39 per run. Some errors were identified related to manager decisions but are considered fixable without altering the core method. The code and workflow are publicly available on GitHub for replication and further experimentation.

items.summary:
Researchers have developed an attack called RAMBO that enables malware on air-gapped computers to generate covert radio signals from memory buses, allowing sensitive data such as files, keylogs, and encryption keys to be leaked. Using software-defined radio hardware and a simple antenna, attackers can intercept and decode these signals from a distance, bypassing traditional network isolation measures.

The study details the design, implementation, and evaluation of this method, achieving data exfiltration rates of up to 1000 bits per second. It also discusses related work and proposes countermeasures to mitigate this novel out-of-band threat to air-gapped systems.

items.title: Report: Big Tech faces stock market pressure over AI spending while bond market continues to finance $1 trillion annual investments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The question we should all be asking about AI
items.summary:
Big Tech companies like Google, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are experiencing stock market declines amid concerns that their massive AI infrastructure investments are not yet profitable. Despite this, the bond market remains willing to finance these companies' AI spending, which JPMorgan estimates has reached $1.6 trillion since 2023 and is expected to hit $1 trillion annually for the next decade.

These companies are borrowing heavily to fund data centers, servers, and other AI infrastructure, with debt financing expected to cover about a third of their capital expenditures this year, totaling around $250 billion. While the bond market currently supports this spending spree, questions remain about how much longer investors will sustain such high levels of lending, especially given competition from other debt markets like US Treasuries.

Smaller AI infrastructure providers, such as neocloud companies, face more financial risk, with some like CoreWeave showing signs of distress and high bond yields. Industry observers note that while hyperscalers appear positioned to benefit from AI demand growth, the broader AI infrastructure market may see significant shakeouts in the near future.

items.originalTitle: AI agent swarms in Minecraft fail to build civilization, drown in bureaucracy
items.summary:
AI researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs conducted experiments with AI agent swarms in Minecraft, deploying 50 agents to collaboratively build a thriving civilization. The agents struggled to progress after initial setbacks, with behaviors resembling bureaucratic inefficiencies, such as prolonged task assignments that hindered development.

The study also compared AI swarms in competitive game modes like Bed Wars and Mindustry, observing differences in strategy and coordination between GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude agents. GPT-based agents demonstrated more aggressive and hive-like cooperation, leading to better performance in combat scenarios. The research aims to inform improvements in multi-agent AI systems by analyzing collaboration and conflict dynamics in controlled gaming environments.

items.originalTitle: Do the math: How we took over ChatGPT accounts
items.summary:
A research team discovered a vulnerability in ChatGPT's sharing feature that allowed attackers to execute malicious JavaScript within the signed-in sessions of users who opened a shared conversation link. This exploit enabled attackers to access private conversations, call authenticated APIs, and effectively take over victims' ChatGPT accounts without requiring any additional actions from the users.

The issue arose from the interaction between ChatGPT's HTML Preview feature and a math library called MathLive, which improperly handled cross-origin messages and failed to sanitize injected HTML content. OpenAI addressed the critical vulnerability, classified as P1, and patched it on October 26, 2026, preventing further exploitation through this method.

They compare AI to an epic narrative that encompasses vast practical knowledge, enabling it to act on the world by drawing from a communal intellectual tradition rather than live intelligence.

Their argument builds on the concept of the "House of Intellect," describing AI models as capturing and deploying the collective, stored human intellect embedded in language and culture. This perspective suggests AI functions as a condensate of human culture, capable of novel applications and self-mobilization, rather than simply parroting human thought or possessing autonomous intelligence.

items.originalTitle: Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds
items.summary:
A study by Vals AI tested 25 Chinese and Western AI models on political questions related to China and found that Chinese models do not uniformly align with Beijing's official positions. The study revealed that language prompts, especially Simplified Chinese, strongly influenced models to produce more pro-government responses, while some Western models occasionally echoed official Chinese stances.

The research showed that most Chinese models rarely refused to answer sensitive questions but sometimes adopted government positions instead. Differences in response formats and usage context also affected political leanings, with models scoring less pro-government when answering yes/no questions or when given system instructions for coding or web search. The study noted that political biases were less apparent in routine tasks but still surfaced in examples like translations and image labeling.

Vals AI highlighted that targeted fine-tuning could reduce pro-government alignment, as seen in a Thomson Reuters model compared to its base version. The findings suggest that Chinese AI models' political behavior is complex and influenced by multiple factors, challenging the assumption that they act solely as government mouthpieces.
